name: Actinic granuloma (annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma)

clinicalPearls: Presents as slowly expanding annular plaques with a raised erythematous border and an atrophic, hypopigmented centre
Lesions characteristically arise on chronically sun-damaged skin such as the face, neck, upper chest and dorsa of the forearms
The condition is closely related to, and by many considered part of the same spectrum as, annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma
Histology shows a granulomatous reaction centred on elastotic (sun-damaged) dermal fibres with multinucleate giant cells engulfing degenerate elastic fibres (elastophagocytosis)
A characteristic feature is loss of elastic tissue in the centre of lesions, accounting for the atrophic appearance
It is generally asymptomatic and follows an indolent course, though lesions may enlarge over months to years
Its relationship to granuloma annulare is debated, but the emphasis on solar elastosis and elastolysis distinguishes it histologically
Treatment is often unsatisfactory; strict photoprotection is advised, with topical or intralesional corticosteroids and other agents tried for cosmetically troublesome disease
reference.pathophysiology: Actinic granuloma is thought to arise from a cell-mediated granulomatous response to ultraviolet-damaged (elastotic) dermal elastic fibres. Chronic sun exposure alters elastic tissue so that it becomes antigenic or is otherwise recognised as abnormal, provoking an infiltrate of histiocytes and multinucleate giant cells that phagocytose the degenerate fibres. The result is destruction and clearance of elastic tissue at the advancing granulomatous border, leaving an elastolytic, atrophic centre. This preferential involvement of sun-damaged skin and the prominent elastophagocytosis distinguish the process from other annular granulomatous dermatoses.
additionalDifferentials: Tinea corporis and other annular infections
Mycosis fungoides presenting with annular plaques
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy demonstrating elastophagocytosis and loss of elastic fibres within a granulomatous infiltrate
Elastic tissue stains to highlight the central loss and giant-cell engulfment of elastic fibres
Mycological examination to exclude dermatophyte infection in annular lesions
Assessment for sarcoidosis when granulomatous histology is found
Review of cumulative sun exposure and photodamage
Autoimmune serology if lupus is suspected clinically
redFlags: Atypical, rapidly enlarging or ulcerating lesions requiring biopsy to exclude malignancy
Granulomatous histology prompting consideration of systemic sarcoidosis
Diagnostic uncertainty with annular lymphoma or lupus
Extensive photodamage warranting surveillance for skin cancer
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and typically follows a slow, indolent course; some lesions resolve spontaneously over years while others persist or slowly enlarge, and treatment responses are variable and often disappointing.
pitfalls: Mistaking the annular lesions for tinea and prescribing ineffective antifungals
Failing to perform elastic tissue stains and missing the characteristic elastolysis
Overlooking the relationship to chronic photodamage and neglecting sun protection
Confusing it with granuloma annulare and misjudging prognosis and associations
management: Rigorous photoprotection with sun avoidance, broad-spectrum sunscreen and protective clothing, addressing the ultraviolet-driven elastolytic process
Topical or intralesional corticosteroids as first-line therapy to suppress the granulomatous inflammation
Alternative options for persistent disease including topical calcineurin inhibitors, antimalarials such as hydroxychloroquine, or systemic agents
Skin biopsy to confirm elastophagocytosis and exclude sarcoidosis, granuloma annulare and dermatophyte infection
Reassurance about the benign, indolent nature and potential for spontaneous resolution, with realistic expectations of variable treatment response
Periodic clinical review to monitor lesion progression or enlargement
